sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Iūnō** (*iuno*) — The Queen of Heaven — belongs to the Roman tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Queenship, Marriage, Sky". The name means "From the same root as Iuppiter, the bright sky"[^1].

Iūnō is not "Hēra with a Latin accent" but a sovereign in her own right: protector of women in every life-stage, keeper of the state's financial memory on the Capitoline, and the one goddess Rome's enemies learned to fear as the will behind the legions.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Iūnō** and serves its temple at [iūnō.com](https://xn--in-wra2j.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *iuno* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Iūnō** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "From the same root as Iuppiter, the bright sky"[^1].

The ASCII form *iuno* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Iūnō** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **i** → **I** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **o** → **ō** — Macron marks the long vowel

The project holds the domain **iūnō.com** (xn--in-wra2j.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro), Aeneid / Eclogues / Georgics, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 19 BCE.
Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈjuː.noː/** — Classical Latin.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: YOO-noh, long ū and long ō.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Latin** — Iūnō
- **Greek twin** — Ἥρα
- **Etruscan** — Uni
- **Owned form** — Iūnō

Latin Iūnō carries two long vowels, and both are preserved in the restoration; the macrons follow Lewis & Short. Her name shares the deep root of iuvenis, "young" — the goddess of the vital force in its prime — which is why her festival, the Kalends, belonged to women at the height of their powers. Old Latin inscriptions write the name IVNO — the consonantal V of Iūnō that the alphabet later split from U.

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.body:
The original script for this roman name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Iūnō** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Iūnō is not "Hēra with a Latin accent" but a sovereign in her own right: protector of women in every life-stage, keeper of the state's financial memory on the Capitoline, and the one goddess Rome's enemies learned to fear as the will behind the legions.[^1]

### Lucina

Iūnō Lucina, "she who brings to light" — the goddess women call in childbirth.

### Moneta

"The Warner" — her Capitoline title; Rome's mint stood in her temple, giving the world the word "money."

### The Geese

Her sacred geese that woke the Capitol in 390 BCE when the Gauls climbed by night.

### Regina

The Queen — third of the Capitoline triad with Iūpiter and Minerva, enthroned on the city's heart-hill.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Iūnō concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The peacock** — Her Argive bird — the hundred eyes of Árgos set in its tail
- **The diadem** — Sovereignty; she rules by right, not by marriage alone
- **The goose** — Vigilance — the alarm the dogs slept through
- **The lily** — In later art, the flower of her maternity

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Roman Iūnō inherits Hēra's jealousy plots but outgrows them: in Rome she is less the wronged wife than the state's queen — a power that must be ritually persuaded, city by city, to change sides.[^1]

### Tantaene Irae (The War)

The Aeneid's engine is her anger: Virgil asks whether heavenly minds can hold such wrath, and answers with seven books of her persecution of Aeneas — the storm off Carthage, the madness of the Italian women, the marriage of Lavinia delayed to blood. When she finally yields, she extracts a condition: the Trojan name shall perish, and only Roman remain. She loses the war and wins the peace.[^2]

### The Goddess Who Changed Sides (The Evocatio)

Before Rome stormed Veii in 396 BCE, the general Camillus performed the evocatio — formally calling the enemy city's Iūnō Regina to abandon Veii for a finer temple in Rome. The Veientine statue, Livy says, nodded assent. Rome conquered Italy partly by inviting its goddesses to defect: Iūnō's transferability made her the instrument of empire's softest power.

### The Geese of the Capitol (The Warning)

When the Gauls scaled the Capitoline cliff by night in 390 BCE, the watchdogs slept — but Iūnō's sacred geese heard them and raised such a clamour that Marcus Manlius woke and threw the first Gaul back down. Rome remembered: dogs were thereafter crucified annually, geese honoured — and Iūnō received the title Moneta, the Warner, beside whose temple the mint later stood.

### Matronalia (The Festival)

On March 1, the old New Year, Roman matrons kept Iūnō Lucina's feast: husbands prayed for wives, slaves were feasted by mistresses, and the temple on the Esquiline — vowed after a plague of stillbirths — received the processions of flowering branches. It was Rome's Mother's Day and its recognition of women's collective religious power.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Her Etruscan form Uni was Rome's first loan: the Capitoline triad itself (Iūpiter, Iūnō, Minerva) is the Etruscan Tinia-Uni-Ménrva. Through evocatio she accumulated the identities of every conquered city's queen — Iūnō Caelestis of Carthage was worshipped in Rome after Carthage burned — and her African form survived into Augustine's polemics. In the Greek East she was simply Hēra again: the empire made her portable in both directions.[^1]

Within the Roman tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[diana|Diāna]], [[ianus|Iānus]], [[iuppiter|Iūppiter]], [[neptunus|Neptūnus]], and [[vulcanus|Vulcānus]].

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Her titles became common nouns: "money" and "monetary" descend from the mint in Moneta's temple; June (Iūnius) bears her name on every calendar; "junoesque" still describes stately beauty. The evocatio — winning by inviting the other side's gods to defect — remains the strangest instrument in the history of religious warfare, and scholars cite it in every discussion of Roman imperialism's flexibility.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The temple of Iūnō Moneta stood on the Arx of the Capitol (349 BCE), where the church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli now rises; the mint's location beside it is the accepted explanation of her name's fortune. Veii's Portonaccio temple — the probable home of the defected Regina — preserves its Etruscan terracottas in the Villa Giulia. Inscribed curses and votives from her Italic sanctuaries (especially at Lanuvium, with its famous serpent cult) document her continuous worship from Latium's earliest towns.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Her titles form a complete biography of Roman womanhood and statecraft.

- **Regina** — 'the Queen'; her Capitoline title as consort of the Optimus Maximus.
- **Lucina** — 'she who brings to light'; the goddess of childbirth, invoked by name in labour.
- **Moneta** — 'the Warner'; from the geese of 390 BCE — and hence, from her mint, the world's word for money.
- **Caprotina** — 'of the wild fig'; her July festival title, when slave-women feasted under the tree.
- **Sospita** — 'the Saviour'; her Lanuvium title, with the serpent and the goat-skin.
- **Curitis** — 'of the spear'; her warrior title among the Sabines.

sources.citation: Ovid, Fasti 3 and 6; Cicero, De Divinatione 1.101.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: The **temple of Iūnō Moneta** crowned the Arx of the Capitol from 344 BCE — vowed after the Gaulish alarm her geese had given — and the Roman mint worked beside it for centuries, which is why money is named for her. **Lanuvium** kept her oldest Latin cult: Iūnō Sospita, whose annual serpent-rite (a virgin offering barley-cakes to the sacred snake, innocence proven by its acceptance) Cicero discusses as a matter of public record. **Carthage's** Caelestis, the Punic queen Rome imported after the city's fall, filled the temple on the Aventine and lasted, Augustine complains, into his own lifetime.

sources.citation: Cicero, De Divinatione 1.79 (Lanuvium); Livy 7.28 (Moneta).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Iūnō is the power that must be persuaded, never merely defeated. Rome's deepest political insight is carved into her story: that legitimacy — of marriage, of money, of the state — is not seized but transferred, and only by consent. Her geese still wake at night in every institution that survives by vigilance rather than force.[^1]

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
